title: Motion of a Satellite — Orbital Velocity and Time Period
topicTitle: Motion of a satellite: orbital velocity and time period of the satellite
notes: **Orbital velocity:** equating gravitational force to centripetal force gives $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$, where $r$ is the orbital radius (distance from Earth's centre). The mass of the satellite cancels out — all satellites at the same radius have the same orbital speed.
**Near Earth's surface:** $v = \sqrt{gR} \approx 7.9\,\text{km/s}$. This is the minimum speed to maintain a circular orbit just above the atmosphere (ignoring air drag).
**Time period:** $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$. This is Kepler's third law in Newtonian form.
**Kepler's third law:** $T^2 \propto r^3$. The square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius. For Earth satellites: $T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$.

**Why higher orbits are slower:** as $r$ increases, $v$ decreases and $T$ increases. The Moon ($r \approx 384,\!400\,\text{km}$) has $v \approx 1.02\,\text{km/s}$ and $T = 27.3\,\text{days}$, while a LEO satellite ($r \approx 6600\,\text{km}$) has $v \approx 7.7\,\text{km/s}$ and $T \approx 90\,\text{min}$.
**Low Earth Orbit (LEO):** altitude $200$–$2000\,\text{km}$. Period $\approx 90$–$120\,\text{min}$. Velocity $\approx 7.8\,\text{km/s}$. Used for ISS, imaging satellites, human spaceflight.
**Medium Earth Orbit (MEO):** altitude $\approx 20,\!000\,\text{km}$. Period $\approx 12\,\text{hours}$. GPS satellites orbit here.
**Orbital energy:** $E = -GMm/2r$. Higher orbits have less negative (higher) energy. To go to a higher orbit, you must ADD energy.
**Derivation of orbital velocity:** $F_{grav} = F_{centripetal} \Rightarrow GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r \Rightarrow v^2 = GM/r \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{GM/r}$.
**Areal velocity:** $dA/dt = L/2m = \text{constant}$ (Kepler's second law). The satellite sweeps equal areas in equal times — moves faster near perigee, slower at apogee.
confusion: Orbital velocity does NOT depend on the mass of the satellite — it depends only on the central mass $M$ and the orbital radius $r$. A feather and a hammer in orbit would have the same orbital speed.

Kepler's third law ($T^2 \propto r^3$) applies to ELLIPTICAL orbits too, with $r$ replaced by the semi-major axis $a$. The constant of proportionality is the same for all satellites of the same central body.

A satellite in a circular orbit is in FREE FALL — it is continuously falling toward Earth but moving forward fast enough to miss it. The occupants feel weightless because both they and the satellite accelerate at the same rate.

To raise a satellite to a higher orbit, you must SPEED UP (fire rockets in the direction of motion) — this seems counterintuitive but is correct. The increased kinetic energy goes into potential energy, and the final orbital speed is actually LOWER.
practice: A satellite orbits Earth at an altitude of $400\,\text{km}$. Find its orbital velocity and period. $R_E = 6400\,\text{km}$, $M_E = 6 \times 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$. Solution: $r = 6800\,\text{km} = 6.8 \times 10^6\,\text{m}$. $v = \sqrt{GM/r} = \sqrt{(6.674 \times 10^{-11})(6 \times 10^{24})/(6.8 \times 10^6)} = 7.67 \times 10^3\,\text{m/s} = 7.67\,\text{km/s}$. $T = 2\pi r/v = 2\pi(6.8 \times 10^6)/(7.67 \times 10^3) = 5575\,\text{s} \approx 93\,\text{min}$.

Find the radius of a geosynchronous orbit (period = 24 hours). $M_E = 6 \times 10^{24}\,\text{kg}$. Solution: $T = 86400\,\text{s}$. $r = \sqrt[3]{GMT^2/(4\pi^2)} = \sqrt[3]{(6.674 \times 10^{-11})(6 \times 10^{24})(86400)^2/(4\pi^2)} = 4.22 \times 10^7\,\text{m} = 42,200\,\text{km}$. Altitude $\approx 35,800\,\text{km}$.

The Moon orbits at $r = 3.84 \times 10^8\,\text{m}$. Verify Kepler's third law: $T^2/r^3$ for Moon and for a LEO satellite ($r = 6.8 \times 10^6\,\text{m}$, $T = 5575\,\text{s}$). Solution: Moon: $T = 27.3 \times 86400 = 2.36 \times 10^6\,\text{s}$. $T^2/r^3 = (2.36 \times 10^6)^2/(3.84 \times 10^8)^3 = 5.57 \times 10^{12}/5.66 \times 10^{25} = 9.84 \times 10^{-14}$. LEO: $T^2/r^3 = (5575)^2/(6.8 \times 10^6)^3 = 3.11 \times 10^7/3.14 \times 10^{20} = 9.9 \times 10^{-14}$. They match.

A satellite in circular orbit of radius $r$ has speed $v$. If its speed is instantaneously increased by $10\%$, what happens? Solution: New speed $v' = 1.1v > v_{circular}$ but $< v_{escape} = \sqrt{2}v \approx 1.414v$. The orbit becomes elliptical with perigee at the burn point and apogee at a larger radius.
universalFacts: Kepler's laws were derived from Tycho Brahe's precise observations. Newton later showed they are consequences of his law of gravitation.
Orbital velocity is independent of the satellite's mass — this was one of Newton's great insights, showing the equivalence of gravitational and inertial mass.

The orbital period of a satellite just above Earth's surface is about $84\,\text{minutes}$ — this is also the period of a simple pendulum of length $R_E$ and the period of oscillation through a tunnel through Earth's centre.
A satellite in low Earth orbit experiences atmospheric drag, which gradually reduces its orbital energy, causing it to spiral inward — eventually it re-enters and burns up.
